transcript:
Header: 2026-04-07 15:00 UTC | Duration: 48m
Attendees: Sofia Martinez (Redwood AE), Liam Chen (Redwood SE), Rachel Park (Nebula Head of ML), David Kim (Nebula Platform), Aisha Patel (Nebula Security)

Summary: Quick walkthrough of Redwood Console tracing, live demo of error analysis and request logs. Customer has intermittent 500 errors showing up in production integration; wants debugging workflow and security assurances.

00:00:05 - Sofia: hey everyone thanks for jumping on, uh quick intros, i'm sofia from redwood, and with me is liam our se who will do most of the console demo. rachel, do you wanna kick off with the problem you're seeing?
00:00:18 - Rachel: yeah thanks sofia. we've been seeing intermittent 500s when our payment orchestration calls go to your hosted api. it's sporadic, like 1 in 2000 requests, not correlated to load. david's got some request ids he can share.
00:00:32 - David: yeah i'll drop a sample in chat after, we captured a request id: rq_20260407_58ab. it's returning a 500 with body "model_error". logs on our side don't have stack trace.
00:00:45 - Liam: cool, that's perfect. i'll show how to map that request id in the console to a trace and then to the underlying request log export. the flow we recommend: grab the request id, search in request logs, then open the trace view to see spans and latency buckets.
00:01:03 - Aisha: quick security note — before we go deep, we need to confirm whether request payloads are stored in plaintext in logs and how long they're retained. also KMS for keys.
00:01:13 - Sofia: yep totally. we'll cover retention settings and KMS. short answer: you can configure retention and integrate with your KMS for key management; we also have RBAC controls for log access. we'll follow up with SOC2 docs after the call.
00:01:27 - Liam: ok jumping into the console — (screen share) — top nav, go to Tracing -> Traces. you can filter by request id, model, route, status code. i'll paste the sample filter we used in the diagnostic run.
00:01:44 - Liam: (narrating) here's the list; you can also aggregate by p50/p95/p99 latency. see this trace with 500 — click to open.
00:01:57 - Liam: trace view shows spans: front-door LB, auth check, request serializer, model call, post-processing. the error span is in "model call" where we saw a typed exception. you can expand span metadata to see the stack excerpt (note: sometimes model stack traces are sanitized).
00:02:16 - Rachel: sometimes our requests include user content with HTML, could that be causing model parsing errors?
00:02:23 - Liam: possibly. in the span metadata we show the input tokenization summary and the length. also the model variant — you can see if fallback to a smaller quantized variant happened. fallbacks can change tokenization behavior.
00:02:40 - David: how does kv cache factor in? we use caching across requests and worry about cache invalidation causing inconsistent results.
00:02:48 - Liam: good Q. KV cache lives on the serving tier. traces include cache hit/miss spans. if KV cache desyncs it could manifest as different model state between requests; trace will show cache miss rate.
00:02:59 - Sofia: also to note, dedicated mode gives you pinned model versions, which reduces variance from fallback.
00:03:06 - Aisha: about logs, can we limit which fields are persisted? we can't store PII in logs.
00:03:13 - Liam: yes — retention & field redaction policies are configurable per workspace. request logs export can redact or omit payload fields; we can run an export example after the call.
00:03:24 - 00:03:30 - (15s gap while Liam navigates)
00:03:30 - Liam: opening request logs tab. here's the schema: timestamp, request_id, route, model, status_code, latency_ms, token_count, user_id (optional), sanitized_input_preview, error_code. you can run ad-hoc queries and export as CSV/JSON.
00:03:46 - David: is the request_id the same across tracing and request logs?
00:03:49 - Liam: yes, we use a unified request id. that maps to trace id; trace may contain multiple spans and internal span ids. so search request logs for rq_20260407_58ab -> the row links to trace view.
00:04:05 - Liam: clicking link now — here's the request row, status 500, latency 312ms, model == gpt-open-13b-q4 (quantized). expanding error details: "model_runtime_exception: tokenization overflow" and a short snippet.
00:04:22 - Rachel: aha tokenization overflow — we do occasionally send very long context in retries.
00:04:27 - Liam: yep that will cause the runtime to fail with 5xx. options: truncate on client, implement prefix caching to reduce input length, or use a model variant with larger context window. we can also add an input sanitizer in the ingestion pipeline to clamp length.
00:04:41 - David: are 5xxs surfaced as retries automatically or do we need to handle?
00:04:45 - Liam: by default the client retries idempotent calls, but for generation calls you'd typically implement application-level retry with backoff. Redwood can be configured to do automatic fallback to a compatible model variant if you enable that policy.
00:04:57 - Aisha: can you show how to trace a sequence where the model fallback happened?
00:05:02 - Liam: sure — filter traces by route and look for span metadata field "fallback_variant": true. (shows examples) here's a case where the query exceeded CPU budget, fallback to gpt-open-6b-q2 happened — note the change in tokenization and longer tail latency.
00:05:22 - 00:05:30 - (crosstalk)
00:05:30 - Rachel: what about cost visibility? we get charged per token but have some low-signal prompts that waste tokens.
00:05:36 - Sofia: Console has token-level cost breakdown per request on the request detail page. you can group by route to find high-cost prompts. Redwood Optimize can recommend prompt truncation or quantization profiles.
00:05:48 - David: for the failing request id, can you show exact raw request payload?
00:05:52 - Liam: depends on retention & redaction settings; in this workspace we have preview only. if you provide consent we can enable full payload retention for a pilot under strict access control. we'll need signoff from Aisha.
00:06:06 - Aisha: ok we'll discuss. for pilot we can enable full retention for selected routes.
00:06:11 - Liam: next, i'll demo the debug timeline. (narrating) timeline shows spans over time; you can play it to see which span is causing the spike. p95 jumps correspond with model call duration.
00:06:27 - Liam: you can also annotate traces with deployment tags (region, instance id) to detect whether an instance-specific issue occurs.
00:06:34 - Rachel: any ways to correlate to infra metrics? we use prometheus.
00:06:38 - Sofia: yes we have integrations. you can pipe trace ids into your APM or use our exported metrics that include instance id and host. mapping's straightforward — we'll share the exporter snippet.
00:06:49 - 00:06:55 - (short pause)
00:06:55 - Liam: now switching to error analysis tab — it groups by error signature. you can click an error and see recent examples, sample requests, and related traces. here's "tokenization overflow" grouped — shows top routes and sample sanitized inputs.
00:07:12 - David: can I export all 500 errors for last 7 days for offline analysis?
00:07:16 - Liam: yes — request logs export lets you filter status_code==500 and export CSV/JSON. you can also include trace links. Exports can be delivered to S3 or downloaded.
00:07:27 - Aisha: for S3 exports, is data encrypted with our KMS?
00:07:31 - Sofia: yes, server-side encryption with customer-managed KMS is supported for export buckets. we can show the required IAM policy snippet.
00:07:40 - Rachel: if we run a pilot with dedicated capacity, how different is the debugging flow?
00:07:45 - Liam: same console, same request id mapping. dedicated just gives pinned models and isolated infra; you'll see less fallback noise. logs are stored in your VPC in Private mode with optional on-prem ingestion.
00:07:57 - Rachel: what's the SLA for dedicated?
00:07:59 - Sofia: we offer SLA-backed uptime and latency targets; details depend on contract, we'll include them in the pricing sheet.
00:08:06 - 00:08:12 - (screen navigation)
00:08:12 - Liam: demoing a live debug: i searched rq_20260407_58ab in request logs — opened trace, found tokenization overflow. then i used the log export to pull last 100 errors; see here where retries caused context to grow.
00:08:28 - Liam: recommended remediation steps: client-side length checks, use prefix caching, or bump model context. also consider enabling auto-fallback to larger model variant for long contexts.
00:08:42 - David: are there automated alerts? we need to be notified when error rate > 0.5%
00:08:47 - Liam: yes — Console alerting supports thresholds on request logs (error_rate, latency p95). you can send to webhook, pagerduty, or email.
00:08:55 - Aisha: audit logs — who can see request logs in our team? we need RBAC to limit access to SREs only.
00:09:01 - Sofia: RBAC roles can be scoped: viewer, operator, security_audit, admin. you can restrict request log access to security_audit role. we also have audit trails of who accessed which trace.
00:09:12 - Rachel: ok this is helpful. david i'll send you the extra request ids.
00:09:15 - David: will do.
00:09:17 - Liam: quick detour on debugging toolchain: if you give us a failing request id we can do a deeper root cause and share a brief incident write-up with traces and suggested remediation. we normally do that as part of pilot onboarding.
00:09:30 - Rachel: sounds good. can we also see tokenization preview across different model variants?
00:09:35 - Liam: yes — in the request detail you can open "tokenization preview" and toggle variants; that helps see why a request may overflow on one variant but not another.
00:09:46 - 00:09:50 - (15s while Liam loads preview)
00:09:50 - Liam: example open — this shows tokens and positions, and where special tokens are added.
00:10:01 - Rachel: excellent.
00:10:03 - Aisha: one more question about compliance — do you keep request logs outside US? we need EU residency for some routes.
00:10:09 - Sofia: yes we have region routing; you can pin routes to EU-only hosting or run in Private VPC in your region. we'll include details in the security package.
00:10:20 - David: what's the expected data retention for request logs by default?
00:10:23 - Liam: default is 30 days for detailed payload previews, 90 days for aggregated metrics, but it's configurable per workspace.
00:10:31 - Rachel: ok next steps?
00:10:34 - Sofia: recap: we'll send security docs (SOC2, KMS integration), pricing and dedicated options, and Liam will spin up a pilot cluster and run initial traces on provided ids. david to share request ids and sample logs. aisha to confirm retention constraints.
00:10:51 - Aisha: noted.
00:10:53 - David: i'll share rq_20260407_58ab and two more ids in chat after call.
00:10:58 - Sofia: perfect. thanks everyone. we'll follow up with an invite for the pilot kickoff.
00:11:05 - (meeting continues with short product questions for 37 more minutes)

11:15:00 - Additional excerpt from later in call (aligned with duration):
00:11:30 - Liam: deep troubleshooting: i pulled the full trace for rq_20260407_58ab, and noticed intermittent memory pressure on the serving host at the exact timestamp. the model runtime emitted a GC spike and then tokenization failed. this is consistent with an edge-case memory fragmentation bug.
00:11:52 - Rachel: is that something you can patch quickly?
00:11:55 - Liam: depends — we have a mitigant: pin to a different instance group or bump memory reservations; long-term fix is an engine patch. for pilot we can avoid the affected instance pool.
00:12:08 - David: any visibility into instance ids in the console?
00:12:11 - Liam: yes instance id tags show up in span metadata; we can filter traces by instance id to find correlated failures.
00:12:20 - Aisha: will this be included in the incident doc?
00:12:22 - Liam: yes, we'll include trace link, spans, instance id, and recommended mitigations in the write-up.
00:12:28 - 00:12:35 - (wrap up)
00:12:35 - Sofia: final recap in chat with next steps and links, thanks all.

End of transcript.
